title: The Castle That Made Kings
subtitle: Warwick Castle → Lord Leycester → the Beauchamp Chapel
intro: One castle, one day, 958 years. Five acts from a Norman earth mound in 1068 to a pair of tombs a ten-minute walk away — three facts to talk about at every stop, and a hard stop at 4 PM.

dayGlance.title: Origins & the Fortress
dayGlance.sub: 9:20 AM — Castle Bridge, the Norman mound, the trebuchet, the towers.

dayGlance.title: The Kingmaker & the House
dayGlance.sub: 11:45 AM — jousting, falconry, the State Rooms, the Mill.

dayGlance.title: Dudley & the Tombs
dayGlance.sub: 2:50 PM — Lord Leycester, then the Beauchamp Chapel. Stop at 4.

acts.label: Act 1 · The Norman beginning
acts.tagline: 1068. An earth mound and a decision.
acts.narrative:
Start outside at Castle Bridge — best view of the castle and it costs nothing. Caesar's Tower comes straight up out of the river, with the arches of the abandoned medieval bridge sitting in the water below.

Then go in and climb the Mound first, because that is literally where the story starts. In 1068 William the Conqueror had been king for two years and still didn't control the Midlands, so he had a mound and a wooden tower thrown up here to hold the road north. Everything else on this site was built on top of that one decision.

acts.label: Act 2 · The fortress
acts.tagline: Three hundred years later, the Beauchamps build in stone.
acts.narrative:
The trebuchet at 10:45 makes one point better than any explanation could: medieval violence was slow. Eighteen metres, twenty-two tonnes, a crew of men and several minutes of winching for a single shot. That was a siege — months of waiting, not battle.

Then the towers. Caesar's Tower and Guy's Tower went up in the 1300s, three hundred years after the mound, when the Beauchamp earls had become one of the richest families in England. They are the reason the place still reads as a fortress from the road.

acts.label: Act 3 · The Kingmaker
acts.tagline: One earl, two kings deposed, dead at 42.
acts.narrative:
This is the centre of the story. Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, put two kings on the throne and took two off it, which is how he ended up remembered as the Kingmaker. He was probably richer than the king he served. He was killed at Barnet in 1471, and four hundred years of family power ended with him.

Falconry at 12:30 closes the outdoor half of the day, and it belongs here more than it first looks — hunting with birds is what earls actually did with their afternoons for five centuries.

acts.label: Act 4 · The long afterlife
acts.narrative:
A castle stays a castle only while somebody needs to defend it. The Grevilles took Warwick in 1604 and spent nearly four hundred years turning a fortress into a house. The Great Hall and State Rooms are that process made visible — and largely a Victorian rebuild, because a fire gutted part of the range in 1871. In 1978 the family sold the whole thing to a waxwork company.

Then the Mill and Engine House down by the river: the least famous thing on the site, where Victorian engineers wired a medieval fortress for electric light.

acts.label: Act 5 · The tombs
acts.tagline: You walked their rooms. Now stand at their graves.
acts.narrative:
Leave the castle at 2:40 and walk into town. The Lord Leycester is a row of crooked timber buildings that began as 14th-century guildhalls; in 1571 Robert Dudley, Elizabeth I's favourite, turned them into a home for wounded and retired soldiers. It still is one, 455 years later. They survived the Great Fire of 1694 that flattened the rest of the centre, which is why they look nothing like the Georgian brick around them.

Then the ending. The Beauchamp Chapel took twenty-one years to build, purely to hold Richard Beauchamp's tomb. Robert Dudley is buried in there too — the same man whose almshouse you walked out of twenty minutes earlier. You spend a whole day inside the rooms these men built and fought over, and then you stand at their graves.

kit: Phone or camera, plus a spare battery — you're recording on and off for six and a half hours
A clip mic or AirPods if you have them — the show arenas are open and windy
Shoes you can climb two towers in
A light layer — 12°C at 9 AM, 20°C by mid-afternoon
Contactless for parking (£10), Lord Leycester (£9) and the chapel (£5)
preTrip: Book the Warwick Castle standard day ticket online tonight — and do NOT add the Dungeon
Do NOT pre-book Lord Leycester — the 25% castle discount only works at their door
Charge every battery, clear the card
Set phone alarms for 10:40, 11:40 and 12:25 — the three shows are the spine of the day
At the gate, check the show board and confirm 10:45 / 11:45 / 12:30 haven't moved
goldenRule: The three shows are fixed points — 10:45, 11:45, 12:30. Everything else bends around them. Miss one and you lose an act.

planArrival.title: Hard stop at 4 PM
planArrival.note: Camera down at the chapel. Eight-minute walk back to the Stables car park, 40 minutes home, in by about 4:50.

castle-bridge.name: Castle Bridge & the River Avon
castle-bridge.angle: Set the scene before you go in
castle-bridge.story: Best view of the castle, and it's free. Caesar's Tower comes straight up out of the river, and the broken arches sitting in the water are the old medieval bridge. Say what the day is: one castle, 958 years, and it ends at their tombs.
facts: There's been a castle on this rock since 1068 — 958 years. Interesting because almost every other English castle fell into ruin; this one never stopped being lived in.
Caesar's Tower has nothing to do with Caesar. The name was made up later because it sounded impressive — medieval marketing.
Those broken arches in the river are the old bridge, abandoned in 1793. They just built a new one next to it and left the old one standing in the water.

routeCard.sub: Castle Bridge, Banbury Road · 9:20 AM · free
routeCard.note: Park first at the Stables car park (CV34 4QU, £10) and walk down — about 5 minutes.

see: The castle's south front in morning light
planCard.todo: Open the video here. One line: this castle made two kings and unmade two. Then walk up to the gate for 10:00.

the-mound.name: The Mound
the-mound.story: This mound is the original castle. William the Conqueror had it thrown up in 1068 to hold the road north, and everything else on the site was built on top of it. Say that and you've set up the next 900 years.
facts: William the Conqueror ordered this in 1068 — two years after Hastings, because he still hadn't got control of the Midlands.
A mound like this went up in weeks, not years: pile earth, put a wooden tower on top, done. Speed was the whole Norman trick — build fast, hold the ground.
Nothing else you can see from up here is Norman. The stone castle came 300 years later, so this mound is the only original piece left.

routeCard.sub: Inside the castle grounds · gates open 10:00
routeCard.note: All the castle stops are one walk, not separate drives.

see: Views over the whole castle site
The grounds Capability Brown landscaped from 1749
planCard.todo: Climb it first, before the site fills up. This is the beginning of the story — keep it to one idea: 1068, one decision, everything follows.

trebuchet.name: The Legend of the Trebuchet
trebuchet.angle: What a siege was actually like
trebuchet.story: One of the biggest working siege engines in the world. The interesting part isn't the shot, it's how long it takes to load — that's the real story of medieval warfare.
facts: 18 metres tall and 22 tonnes, built from medieval drawings — one of the largest working siege machines anywhere.
It takes a crew several minutes to load one shot. That tells you what a siege really was: months of sitting around, not battle.
Trebuchets didn't only throw stones — they threw dead animals over the walls to spread disease. Biological warfare, 700 years early.

routeCard.sub: River bank, below the castle · 10:45 show
routeCard.note: Included in your day ticket. Get there 5 minutes early for a clear sightline.

planCard.todo: Get there for 10:45. Watch the loading, not just the launch — that's the point you want to make.

towers.name: Guy's Tower, Caesar's Tower & the Ramparts
towers.angle: 300 years later, the family gets rich
towers.story: Caesar's Tower and Guy's Tower are the reason the place still looks like a fortress. They went up in the 1300s when the Beauchamp earls had the money to build in stone. Climb both and walk the wall between them.
facts: Both towers are 14th century — 300 years after the mound. They got built when the Beauchamp family became one of the richest in England.
Caesar's Tower has a dungeon in the basement that held French knights captured at Poitiers in 1356. Prisoners weren't enemies, they were ransom money.
Guy's Tower is twelve-sided, not square. Corners could be undermined by attackers, so the shape itself was a defence.

routeCard.note: Steep, narrow spiral stairs and no lift. Take it slowly.

walkPoints.name: Guy's Tower
walkPoints.story: Twelve-sided, about 39 metres, five storeys of guest chambers stacked above each other. Built to impress as much as defend.
walkPoints.todo: Climb this one first while your legs are fresh.

walkPoints.name: The ramparts
walkPoints.story: The curtain wall walk linking the two great towers, looking down into the courtyard on one side and out over the Avon on the other.
walkPoints.todo: Walk it slowly — best views over the river and down into the courtyard.

walkPoints.name: Caesar's Tower
walkPoints.story: The taller of the two at roughly 44 metres, with a dungeon in the basement that held French knights captured at Poitiers in 1356.
walkPoints.todo: Mention the dungeon and the French prisoners. It lands better than the height does.

see: Views over the Avon and the courtyard
planCard.todo: Both towers and the wall between them in 30 minutes. Steep, narrow stairs. Be down and seated for the jousting at 11:45.

jousting.name: Wars of the Roses LIVE
jousting.angle: The man who made and unmade kings
jousting.story: This is the centre of the whole story. Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, is remembered as the Kingmaker because he put two kings on the throne and took two off it. Tell that before the show starts, then let the horses do the rest.
facts: Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, deposed two kings and installed two others. That's literally why they call him the Kingmaker.
He was probably richer than the king he served — which is exactly how one subject ends up powerful enough to swap monarchs.
He was killed at the Battle of Barnet in 1471, and Warwick's power died with him. One battle ended 400 years of family dominance.

routeCard.note: Included in the day ticket. Seats fill — get there by 11:40.

see: The castle's south front as backdrop
planCard.todo: Tell the Kingmaker story before it starts, while the arena is filling. Then watch.

falconry.name: The Falconer's Quest
falconry.angle: The most expensive hobby in medieval Europe
falconry.story: Biggest bird of prey display in the country. It isn't part of the castle's story exactly, but hunting with birds is what earls actually did all afternoon for 500 years, so it fits.
facts: Falconry was ranked by law — the bird you were allowed to fly depended on your rank. An eagle for a king, a kestrel for a servant.
A trained hawk could cost more than a horse. This was the most expensive thing a medieval noble did for fun.
'Fed up', 'hoodwinked' and 'under his thumb' are all falconry terms. They're still in everyday English 500 years later.

routeCard.note: Included in the day ticket. Sit on the grassed slope for the cleanest sky behind the birds.

see: Eagles, vultures and owls in flight
planCard.todo: Last outdoor stop. After this the weather stops mattering for the rest of the day.

lunch.name: Lunch — thirty minutes
lunch.angle: Halfway, and the hard part is already filmed
lunch.story: Halfway. All three shows are done and the outdoor half of the day is behind you. Everything from here is indoors.

routeCard.sub: Inside the castle grounds · 30 minutes, no longer

see: Somewhere to sit down for half an hour
planCard.todo: Thirty minutes, not an hour. Sit down properly — you've been on your feet since 9:20.

state-rooms.name: Great Hall & State Rooms
state-rooms.angle: When a fortress stops being a fortress
state-rooms.story: A castle only stays a castle while somebody needs to defend it. The Greville family took over in 1604 and spent nearly 400 years turning it into a house. This is where the story stops being about war and starts being about money and showing off.
facts: The Greville family held this castle for 374 years, from 1604 to 1978. Nobody needed to defend it any more, so they turned it into a home.
A fire in 1871 gutted part of it, so a lot of what you walk through is Victorian rebuild pretending to be much older.
In 1978 they sold it to Madame Tussauds — the waxwork company. That's how a Norman fortress ended up a visitor attraction.

routeCard.note: Low light indoors — handheld, brace against door frames rather than pushing the ISO.

planCard.todo: Say the turn out loud: this is the point the castle stops being a weapon and becomes a house.

mill-engine.name: Mill & Engine House
mill-engine.angle: The only part built for work
mill-engine.story: Down by the river under Caesar's Tower. The Victorians put generators in here to light the castle. Least famous thing on the site and one of the most interesting.
facts: The Victorians installed generators here, so the castle had electric light before most of Warwick town did.
The mill site itself is medieval — the same spot powered by water, then by electricity, 700 years apart.
It's the only part of the castle built for work rather than war or for show.

routeCard.note: Steps down and back up. Last castle stop — leave by 2:40 for the walk into town.

see: The medieval bridge arches from the far bank
planCard.todo: Quick stop. The broken bridge arches from this morning are right outside — same subject from the other bank.

lord-leycester.name: The Lord Leycester
lord-leycester.angle: The other man in this story
lord-leycester.story: Ten minutes' walk from the gate. A row of crooked timber buildings that Robert Dudley turned into a home for old soldiers in 1571. You need to introduce him here, because you're about to stand at his tomb.
facts: Robert Dudley founded this in 1571 as a home for wounded soldiers — and it still houses ex-servicemen 455 years later.
Dudley was Elizabeth I's favourite and probably hoped to marry her. A public good deed like this was how you built a reputation at court.
The buildings are 14th-century guildhalls that survived the Great Fire of 1694. That's why everything around them is Georgian brick and these are timber.

routeCard.sub: High Street · open till 5, last admission 4
routeCard.note: Buy at the door, NOT online — the 25% castle discount only works at their ticket office.

planCard.todo: Show your Warwick Castle ticket at the desk for 25% off — £9 instead of £12. Introduce Dudley here.

beauchamp-chapel.name: St Mary's — The Beauchamp Chapel
beauchamp-chapel.angle: The ending — they're all in this one room
beauchamp-chapel.story: This is where the day ends. The chapel was built to hold one man's tomb, and Robert Dudley is in here too — the same man whose almshouse you just left. You've spent the day in the rooms these men built, and now you're standing at their graves. Say that, then stop.
facts: This chapel took 21 years to build, 1443 to 1464, purely to house one man's tomb — Richard Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick.
His effigy is gilt bronze with the hands raised but not joined together. That's deliberate: he's shown seeing a vision, not praying.
Robert Dudley is buried here too — the man whose almshouse you walked out of twenty minutes ago. The whole day ends in one room.

routeCard.note: Open from 10:30 on Saturdays and closes at 5, so 3:30 is comfortable. Chapel and chancel are £5 on the door.

planCard.todo: Pay the £5 for the chapel — this is the ending, not an extra. Say your closing line here and finish.

coldOpen.title: Cold open
coldOpen.where: Castle Bridge, before you go in — 9:20 AM
facts: The hook: 'this castle made two kings, and unmade two kings'
What this is: one castle, one day, 958 years
The promise: by the end of this video you'll be standing at their graves

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
signOff.where: In the Beauchamp Chapel, or on the church steps — 3:55 PM
facts: One sentence: whose tomb this is and why he mattered
The link back: 'that's the castle we started at this morning'
The ask: like, subscribe — and where should the next one go?

talkTipbox: Three facts per stop, and you only need to land the one that interests you most. Say the date, say what happened, say why it's odd or surprising — then move on. You're walking, talking and recording at the same time, so short beats complete every time.
goldenRules: Three fixed show times: 10:45 trebuchet, 11:45 jousting, 12:30 falconry. Everything bends around them.
Confirm those times on the board at the gate — they do move.
Keep your castle ticket on you: it's 25% off at Lord Leycester (£9 not £12).
£5 cash or card for the Beauchamp Chapel — that's the ending, don't skip it.
Talk before each show starts, not over the top of it.
Hard stop at 4 PM. Lord Leycester's last admission is 4; St Mary's shuts at 5.
outro: One castle, 958 years, and you finish standing at their tombs. That's a film, not a tour.
